segs.text: Did humanity's birthplace have something special? The oldest known fossils of the human line, and of our own species, come from Africa. That part is well established. The open question is why. This is Open Questions, episode three. Every study on screen is published, and its source is on screen too.

First, what the fossils show. At Laetoli, in Tanzania, footprints about three point seven million years old were pressed into volcanic ash. Most researchers attribute them to Lucy's species, Australopithecus afarensis. At Olduvai Gorge, also in Tanzania, Mary Leakey found a skull of an early human relative in nineteen fifty-nine, in a layer later dated to about one point eight million years. Fossils from early in the history of our own species come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about three hundred thousand years old, and Omo Kibish in Ethiopia, at least about two hundred thirty thousand.

Genetics points the same way. People in Africa carry more genetic variation than people anywhere else, and variation elsewhere is largely a subset of it. In two thousand seventeen, Carina Schlebusch and colleagues, in Science, estimated, using genetic models, that the deepest split among living human populations happened roughly three hundred fifty to two hundred sixty thousand years ago. An African origin is well supported. Why there, and where in Africa, is not.

So there are two broad kinds of explanation. One says the place mattered: Africa, especially the Rift Valley region, had conditions that pushed our ancestors to adapt. The other says the record is skewed: fossils survive and get found there, so the true map may be wider. They are not exclusive.

First, the place mattered. The Rift is a chain of valleys where the crust is pulling apart, putting lakes, highlands and volcanoes close together. In nineteen ninety-eight, Richard Potts proposed that unstable environments like this favored species able to adapt rather than specialize. In twenty eighteen, Potts and colleagues, in Science, reported that at Olorgesailie, in Kenya, shifting climate and tectonic activity coincided with animal turnover and a new stone toolkit. That is a correlation at one site. Whether it explains our origin is still a hypothesis.

Second, the record is skewed. Fossils form best with fast burial. Rift basins collect sediment. Volcanoes drop ash that seals sites and can be dated by potassium-argon and argon-argon methods. Faulting and erosion then expose old layers, as the river did at Olduvai. In humid forests, acidic soil and scavengers destroy bones. So the Rift can be a good archive without being the only place early humans lived.

Gaps and delays have happened before. In nineteen twenty-five, Raymond Dart described the Taung Child from South Africa, and it was widely doubted for years, partly over what experts expected about human origins. Until two thousand five, no fossil chimpanzee had been reported anywhere. Then Sally McBrearty and Nina Jablonski described chimpanzee teeth about half a million years old from Kenya's Rift Valley. And in twenty ten, the Denisovans were first identified from DNA in a Siberian finger bone.

A third view widens the map. Jebel Irhoud in Morocco lies thousands of kilometers from Omo in Ethiopia. In twenty eighteen, Eleanor Scerri and colleagues, in Trends in Ecology and Evolution, argued that our species may have emerged from many partly connected populations across Africa, rather than one cradle. That is an interpretation, not a settled result.

Now, a different question: survival. About seventy-four thousand years ago, the Toba volcano in Sumatra erupted, one of the largest eruptions of the last two million years. In nineteen ninety-eight, Stanley Ambrose proposed that its volcanic winter cut human numbers to a small group of survivors. This is the Toba catastrophe hypothesis.

Several studies pushed back. In two thousand seven, Michael Petraglia and colleagues, in Science, reported stone tools in India both below and above the Toba ash, with no clear break. In twenty thirteen, Christine Lane and colleagues found Toba ash in Lake Malawi sediment with no sign of a volcanic winter in East Africa. In twenty eighteen, Eugene Smith and colleagues, in Nature, reported people living on the South African coast through the eruption. A few sites cannot show how everyone fared, so this stays contested.

What would narrow it down? Searching places that preserve poorly or are little explored, such as West and Central Africa. Dating more sites precisely. Recovering ancient proteins, which can outlast DNA in warm climates. And comparing more genomes, ancient and living.

So what does this show? Established: the oldest known fossils of our species are in Africa, genetics agrees our species began there, and volcanic ash at Rift sites lets many fossil-bearing layers be dated. Not established: whether Africa's conditions caused our origin or only revealed it, whether our species began in one region or across a network, and whether Toba nearly ended us. Scientists disagree on each.

This does not settle whether Africa was special. A map of fossils is partly a map of preservation and of searching. Scientists still argue about how much of the pattern is real, and how much is the record.
